title: Officers’ donations inside the contractor window, against the campaign calendar
question: Officers of City contractors gave to committees of the officials who approve their contracts inside the period the ban covers. Is that more often than the timing of campaigns and approvals alone would produce?
finding: Campaign filings from 2017 to 2026 hold 248 donations to a committee of the approving office by a person who is named on a contractor’s notice and gave that contractor as employer. 53 of them ($13,400) fall from 180 days before to 365 days after an approval, and 26 fall in the 365 days after one, the part of the period that needs no guess about when a proposal went in. Because many of these contractors have an approval every year, their windows cover much of the calendar: if these donors gave on the same days as every other donor to the same committees, 52 of the 248 would fall inside. The count is no more than the calendar alone gives. 5 of the 53 are followed by a refund entry for the same donor and committee.
how: Officers, directors and owners are the people each notice lists (subcontractors left out). A donation is kept only when the donor’s first and last name match a listed person AND the employer the donor gave matches the contractor’s name; it must be an individual’s contribution on Schedule A to a committee whose name carries “supervisor” (for a Board approval) or the approving officer’s surname (for the Mayor or another officer). Only approvals whose own notice lists the donor count. For each donor and contractor the windows from 180 days before to 365 days after each such approval are merged, and the share of ALL contributions to that class of committee that fall on covered days is that pair’s calendar share. The expected count is the sum of those shares over every kept donation, inside a window or not. Each donation is counted once however many approvals are near it; an employer entry must be at least four letters long to match by being part of the contractor’s name (so “N/A” does not match “Institute on Aging”), and a name that boils down to one common word (“Foundation”) does not match inside a longer one; public bodies named as contractors are left out; a notice in the 2026 filing system is tied to the Mayor in office on the approval date rather than to the staff member who signed it; and a Retirement Board approval is tied only to the elective officer who sits on that board. “Before a notice was on file” means after the approval and before the notice naming the donor was signed.
limits: The 180 days before approval stand in for the date a proposal was submitted, which the notices do not give; only the 365 days after approval are certain to be inside the ban, and only for a contract of $100,000 or more in a fiscal year. A name and employer match is strong evidence of identity, not proof. The board and officer names are those printed on the contract notice, which can repeat an old board list, so a listed person may have left the board, or not yet joined it, on the date of a donation. The comparison says whether the timing is unusual; it does not say whether any one donation was permitted, since the ban does not depend on how often others give. Sums are small (most are $500 or less). The everyday reason is that people who run City-funded organizations take part in local politics all year.
